$schema-note: Hand-maintained. Data, not code: nothing under src/ imports this file.
purpose: The guard ledger for WIN-258 TRANCHE 5 — `skills`' canonical store, the
NINTH owner behind the one PostgreSQL client ADR M0.3 §15 gives the ORM.
One entry per guard: per scope predicate, per vocabulary check that stands
where no enum stands, per shape check that stands where a migration-only
CHECK stands, per envelope decision that keeps a row an older binary wrote
readable, and per clause of a statement the port's contract depends on.
Each carries the file it lives in, the EXACT text that implements it
(`from`), the edit that removes it (`to`), and the NAMED cases that were
seen to go red (`kills`).
IT IS A TENTH FILE beside mutations.json, mutations-identity.json,
mutations-ports.json, mutations-outbox.json, mutations-tools.json,
mutations-agents.json, mutations-cost.json, mutations-channels.json,
mutations-governance.json and mutations-secrets.json rather than an
extension of any of them, for the reason the fourth was: ten tranches are
ten separate claims about ten separate port surfaces, and a reader checking
one should not have to read past the other nine. All are hashed by the same
packages.adapters.config rule and counted together by the v1 ledger.
WHY THIS TRANCHE NEEDED ITS OWN SWEEP. THREE columns of this context are
typed far more loosely in PostgreSQL than in the domain and NOTHING in the
database narrows them. `Skill.origin` is a plain TEXT with the closed set
living only in `domain/manifest.ts`; `Skill.manifest` is JSONB behind ONE
check on its ROOT, so no field inside it is checked at all; and
`Skill.providesTools` is JSONB behind one check on its root and is the
column `domain/catalogue.ts` says the RUNTIME reads in preference to the
manifest. A store that CAST any of the three would hand a caller a value
outside its own type with no error anywhere.
AND THREE TEXT[] COLUMNS ARE NULLABLE IN THE DDL AND NON-OPTIONAL IN
`schema.prisma`. `00000000000000_initial/migration.sql` declares `tags`,
`requiredEnvironmentKeys` and `optionalEnvironmentKeys` as
`TEXT[] DEFAULT ARRAY[]::TEXT[]` with no NOT NULL on any of them, while the
generated types present all three as `String[]`. A row holding SQL NULL is
representable, the type system denies that it is, and the in-memory double
— which holds JavaScript arrays — cannot produce one at all.
SEVEN NAMED CASES EXIST BECAUSE THIS LEDGER WAS ENUMERATED FIRST. Five
guards had no case anywhere that could go red: the uuid guard on the PATCH
path, the project and organization halves of a binding read, the
`organizationId` clause of the raw anonymisation UPDATE, the re-enable half
of both install upserts, and `jsonb_set(create_missing => true)`. Two of
those five are guards NOTHING THAT GOES THROUGH THE PORT CAN REACH — the
port has no disable method and no way to write a manifest without an author
— so their cases plant the input as SQL, which is the only honest way to
build it.
procedure: PROVE THE SUITES GREEN FIRST. Tranche 1's first sweep reported 22 kills and
every one was VACUOUS: a context's `dist` had been cleaned, so every suite
failed to load its import and would have 'died' against any mutation at
all, including none. The driver runs each suite set UNMUTATED and refuses
to sweep unless it is green with a non-zero executed case count, and
classifies a run with no executed cases as VACUOUS rather than as a kill.
THE INTEGRATION SUITES RUN ON A REAL POSTGRESQL, in a container, on the
machine that has a daemon. `skills-rows.test.ts` is the only suite here
that runs without one, and it is the one that reaches the mapping branches
a container suite cannot: a container only ever reads rows THIS BINARY
WROTE, so the legacy-manifest, unknown-origin and NULL-array branches are
unreachable from it except through the rows the rules suite plants as raw
EVERY `from` IS A UNIQUE SUBSTRING OF ITS FILE and is applied literally, so
a mutation that failed to match is reported as UNAPPLIED rather than

mutations.name: M-K03 rows: a TEXT[] element is text, checked rather than assumed
mutations.from: if (typeof element !== "string") refuse(UNREADABLE_TEXT_LIST, `${field} holds a non-text element`);

mutations.name: M-K04 rows: a REQUIRED manifest key is present and is text
mutations.from: if (typeof value !== "string") refuse(UNREADABLE_MANIFEST, `${field}.${key} is missing or is not text`);
mutations.to: if (false) refuse(UNREADABLE_MANIFEST, `${field}.${key} is missing or is not text`);
mutations.note: `Skill.manifest` is JSONB behind ONE check on its ROOT. Nothing checks a field inside it, so a manifest with no `id` reads back as a `SkillManifest` whose slug is undefined.

mutations.name: M-K05 rows: a NULLABLE manifest key present with the wrong type is refused
mutations.from: if (typeof value !== "string") refuse(UNREADABLE_MANIFEST, `${field}.${key} is present and is not text`);
mutations.to: if (false) refuse(UNREADABLE_MANIFEST, `${field}.${key} is present and is not text`);
mutations.note: The distinction this guard makes is the whole expand/contract discipline: an ABSENT key is version skew and normalises to null, a key PRESENT with the wrong type is corruption. Collapsing them hides the second.

mutations.note: `required_env`, `optional_env` and `tags` are required properties of `SkillManifest` and a manifest serialised before one of them existed has no key at all. Refusing it makes this binary unable to read what an older one wrote.

mutations.name: M-K07 rows: manifest.origin is validated against the closed set
mutations.note: The manifest carries its own `origin` beside the column's, and `resolveOrigin` reads it as the second precedence step of a REGISTRATION. A value outside the union there decides the official flag of the next re-registration.

mutations.name: M-K08 rows: an UNKNOWN manifest key survives a read
mutations.note: The CONTRACT direction of expand/contract. Rebuilding the manifest from a known key list silently DELETES a newer release's field on the next write, and `upsertSkill` writes the manifest it was handed.

mutations.name: M-K09 rows: an UNKNOWN provided-tool field survives a read
mutations.note: Same direction, on the column the RUNTIME reads. `domain/catalogue.ts` says `providesTools` is read back in preference to the manifest, so a dropped field is a field the sandbox never sees.

mutations.name: M-K10 rows: a provided tool has a NAME
mutations.from: if (typeof name !== "string") refuse(UNREADABLE_PROVIDED_TOOLS, `${field} element has no tool name`);
mutations.to: if (false) refuse(UNREADABLE_PROVIDED_TOOLS, `${field} element has no tool name`);
mutations.note: The name is what `domain/tool-namespace.ts` folds the slug into. A nameless element becomes a namespaced tool called `slug__undefined`, offered to the runtime.

mutations.name: M-K11 rows: a provided tool's schema is an object or null
mutations.from: if (!isPlainObject(value)) refuse(UNREADABLE_PROVIDED_TOOLS, `${field} element schema is not an object`);
mutations.to: if (false) refuse(UNREADABLE_PROVIDED_TOOLS, `${field} element schema is not an object`);
mutations.note: `inputSchema` is handed to the executor as a JSON Schema. An array or a string there is a schema no dialect can read, and this context does not interpret it, so nothing downstream would notice.

mutations.name: M-K13 rows: manifest has an OBJECT root
mutations.from: if (!isPlainObject(value)) refuse(UNREADABLE_MANIFEST, "Skill.manifest is not an object");
mutations.to: if (false) refuse(UNREADABLE_MANIFEST, "Skill.manifest is not an object");
mutations.note: The counterpart of `Skill_manifest_json_root`, on the read side.

mutations.name: M-K14 rows: EnvironmentSkill.config has an OBJECT root
mutations.from: if (!isPlainObject(value)) refuse(UNREADABLE_INSTALL_CONFIG, "EnvironmentSkill.config is not an object");
mutations.to: if (false) refuse(UNREADABLE_INSTALL_CONFIG, "EnvironmentSkill.config is not an object");
mutations.note: The counterpart of `EnvironmentSkill_config_json_root`. The config is the tenant's own per-environment settings and is handed to the sandbox verbatim.

mutations.name: M-K15 guards: the uuid shape is the canonical hyphenated form
mutations.note: Four columns are `@db.Uuid` and this context's own doubles mint `org-1` and `id-0001`. Without the shape check the string reaches `uuid_in`, and the driver's raise inside a caller's transaction takes the TRANSACTION as well as the answer.

mutations.note: Two migration-only CHECKs stand behind this one function. Letting the value through means the database raises instead — and a raise aborts the caller's whole transaction, which is the difference between a refusal and an incident.

mutations.name: M-K20 guards: a TEXT[] write refuses a non-text element
mutations.note: The write half of M-K03. The column has no element constraint at all.

mutations.name: M-K21 guards: an empty segment of the uniqueness key is refused
mutations.note: Neither `slug` nor `version` carries a CHECK, which is exactly why the guard is here: an empty version does not FAIL, it SUCCEEDS, and every version-less registration in the organization then converges onto that one row and overwrites the last.

mutations.name: M-K22 guards: an unrepresentable instant is refused
mutations.note: An `Invalid Date` reaches the driver as NaN and is reported as a parameter error with no column named.

mutations.name: M-K23 visibility: the install clause spans BOTH levels
mutations.note: `domain/visibility.ts`: 'a skill installed in the project but not bound in this environment is NOT visible here. Checking only the project half would leak a staging-only skill into production.'

mutations.name: M-K24 visibility: the organization match is a CONJUNCT, not a fallback
mutations.from:
organizationId: scope.environment.organizationId,
    OR: [{ isOfficial: true }, installedHere(scope)],
mutations.note: 'Official' means catalogue-owned, not global. Without the conjunct every official row in the installation is visible from every environment of every tenant.

mutations.name: M-K25 visibility: an official row is visible with no install at all
mutations.note: It is what makes a fresh environment able to run the seeded catalogue before anyone has installed anything, and what `shouldMaterialiseInstall` is written around.

mutations.name: M-K26 visibility: official rows sort FIRST
mutations.note: The first comparison of `compareCatalogueEntries`. PostgreSQL orders false before true, so DESC is what puts official first; the pin is the ordering the library surface reads.

mutations.name: M-K27 visibility: a slug's HIGHEST version wins
mutations.note: The port says a slug names a FAMILY of rows and an implementation MUST return the highest version. `findVisibleSkillByReference` is `findFirst` over this order, so the direction IS the rule.

mutations.name: M-K28 visibility: a search term is TRIMMED
mutations.note: `matchesSearch` trims and the client does not, so an untrimmed ' web' matches nothing in SQL and everything containing `web` in the double.

mutations.name: M-K29 visibility: a null search is no filter at all
mutations.note: Without it `null.trim()` throws a TypeError, which `refuseSkills` deliberately RETHROWS — so every unfiltered page read rejects rather than answering.

mutations.name: M-K30 visibility: a reference that is not a uuid is not sent to uuid_in

mutations.note: `Skill.id` is `@db.Uuid` and a slug is the ordinary input to this method. An unguarded id arm makes every slug lookup a driver error, and a driver error inside a transaction aborts the transaction.

mutations.name: M-K32 catalogue: a re-registration does not move createdAt
mutations.note: 'A row that looks new after every edit is a row nobody can audit.' The identity triple is the uniqueness key, so a re-registration is the SAME row and its origin instant is a fact about the row rather than about the write.

mutations.name: M-K33 catalogue: a re-registration OVERWRITES what the manifest describes
mutations.note: `revisionFrom` names exactly the columns a re-registration replaces. An upsert that only touched the timestamp would accept a new manifest and keep serving the old prompt block.

mutations.name: M-K34 catalogue: a patch of an unknown id is a refusal, not a crash
mutations.note: `updateManyAndReturn` answers an empty array rather than raising, which is why it is used instead of `update`; without the check the empty array reaches `readSkill` and the method rejects.

mutations.name: M-K35 catalogue: a patch of a NON-UUID id is a refusal, not an aborted transaction
mutations.note: The write-path half of the uuid guard, and the expensive one: `updateManyAndReturn({ where: { id } })` sends the string to `uuid_in` inside the caller's own transaction.

mutations.name: M-K36 catalogue: the official flag is what hasOfficialSkills asks about
mutations.note: It drives LAZY SEEDING. Answering true for any catalogue row at all means a fresh organization never gets its official skills.

mutations.name: M-K37 catalogue: hasOfficialSkills is confined to ONE organization
mutations.from:
where: { organizationId: organization.organizationId, isOfficial: true },
          select: { id: true },
mutations.to:
where: { isOfficial: true },
          select: { id: true },
mutations.note: The seeding decision is per organization. Without the clause the FIRST organization to be seeded suppresses seeding for every other one in the installation.

mutations.name: M-K38 catalogue: a page's TOTAL is of the filter, not of the window
mutations.from: return ok({ items: rows.map((row) => readSkill(row as SkillRow)), total });
mutations.to: return ok({ items: rows.map((row) => readSkill(row as SkillRow)), total: rows.length });
mutations.note: The port says so, and the consequence is concrete: a caller paging on a windowed total never reaches the last page.

mutations.name: M-K39 catalogue: skills resolved FROM installations are still visibility-filtered
mutations.note: A caller holding an install it resolved under one scope must not be able to read another organization's catalogue row by handing it back under a different one.

mutations.name: M-K40 installs: an adoption checks the scope before it writes
mutations.note: `ProjectSkill.projectId` is written straight from the scope and `ProjectSkill_ancestry` then checks it against the SKILL's organization — a check that cannot see a scope whose own levels disagree.

mutations.name: M-K41 installs: both upserts RE-ENABLE
mutations.from:
update: { enabled: true, updatedAt: at },
          select: PROJECT_SKILL_COLUMNS,
mutations.note: `domain/installation.ts`: 'a re-install is the documented way to undo a disable'. The port has no disable METHOD, so nothing that goes through it can produce the input — which is why the case that kills this plants a disabled row as SQL.

mutations.name: M-K42 installs: the environment upsert re-enables too
mutations.from:
update: { enabled: true, updatedAt: at },
          select: ENVIRONMENT_SKILL_COLUMNS,
mutations.note: The second half of the same rule, on the row that actually gates a turn.

mutations.name: M-K43 installs: a binding read joins through the PROJECT, not the environment alone
mutations.note: `EnvironmentSkill` carries `environmentId` and `projectSkillId` and nothing above either, so the project and organization halves of a read's scope are the CALLER'S claim and nothing in the row checks them.

mutations.name: M-K44 installs: a bulk resolve answers in the CALLER'S order and repeats a repeated id
mutations.to: return ok(rows.map((row) => hydrate(row as InstallationRow, scope)));
mutations.note: A bare `IN` answers in whatever order the plan produced; the double answers in the order it was ASKED. A store that returned the rows as they arrived would diverge on a list of two, silently, in the method the runtime load goes through.

mutations.name: M-K45 installs: a non-uuid binding id is dropped rather than sent
mutations.note: ONE bad element in an `IN` list aborts the whole statement — and, inside a transaction, the transaction with it. The port already says a binding this scope does not cover is simply absent.

mutations.name: M-K46 installs: an uninstall answers whether it removed anything
mutations.note: The port's answer is a boolean about the ROW, and the tenant-facing surface reports 'uninstalled' from it. A constant true reports work that did not happen.

mutations.name: M-K47 installs: an uninstall reaches only THIS environment's binding
mutations.note: 'Uninstalling from staging must not uninstall from production.' Without the environment clause one tenant's uninstall removes the binding in every environment that adopted the same catalogue row.

mutations.name: M-K48 installs: a non-uuid skill id does not reach an uninstall statement
mutations.note: The write path again: a DELETE whose predicate raises takes the caller's transaction.

mutations.name: M-K49 erasure: a project-level selector selects NOTHING
mutations.note: `Skill` is organization-scoped and the double resolves the selector by the kernel's `contains` with the SELECTOR as the outer scope, so only an organization path contains `org/<id>`. Transcribed rather than corrected: changing it would make an erasure erase MORE rows against PostgreSQL than against the store every use-case suite is written against.

mutations.name: M-K50 erasure: a subject with no principal selects nothing
mutations.note: An end-user or an entity subject has no `author` column to match. Without the guard the selector becomes `author: null`, which matches every skill nobody claimed.

mutations.name: M-K51 erasure: the anonymisation is confined to ONE organization
mutations.note: An erasure addressed at one tenant would otherwise rewrite the author of every skill in the installation carrying the same principal string.

mutations.name: M-K52 erasure: the anonymisation is confined to the SUBJECT
mutations.note: Without the clause one subject's erasure anonymises every authored skill in the organization, and the count it returns is the size of the catalogue.

mutations.name: M-K53 erasure: the stored MANIFEST is overwritten as well as the column
mutations.note: The name is in two places. `domain/manifest.ts` fixes the frontmatter field names as the persisted contract, and overwriting only the column leaves the name legible in the JSON — which reads as complete, because the column says [erased].

mutations.name: M-K54 erasure: jsonb_set CREATES the key when a manifest never carried one
mutations.note: A row written before `author` was in the frontmatter has the name in the COLUMN and no key in the JSON. With `false` the anonymisation leaves the JSON untouched.

mutations.name: M-K55 refusal: a TransactionScopeError is RETHROWN, never folded into a Result
mutations.note: The three scope refusals are the property tranche 1 built and every tranche since relies on. Converting them to a `Result` lets a use case that lost its transaction carry on as though a row had merely failed to write.

mutations.name: M-K56 refusal: the distinct CODE leads the reason a caller receives
mutations.note: `domain/errors.ts` publishes ONE caller-facing code for every store failure, deliberately. The discrimination therefore has to travel in `details.reason`, led by the code, or an operator cannot tell thirteen refusals apart.

mutations.name: M-K57 stamps: the instant source never repeats
mutations.note: `createdAt` and `updatedAt` are timestamp(3), so two rows written in the same millisecond TIE — and `now()` would be worse, because on PostgreSQL it is the TRANSACTION'S start time and every row a seeding run wrote in one unit of work would carry the identical instant.

mutations.name: M-K58 stamps: every minted identifier is a uuid
mutations.note: All three primary keys are `@db.Uuid`. A source that minted anything else is refused by the guard one line earlier and by the column one statement later.
